subtopic: USE OF HUTS AND TENTS BY ACTIVE AND RESERVE UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was asked a question by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) regarding the use of huts and tents by the active army and the reserve army. The information which I have received is that two advanced training centres are being established at Petawawa, one an artillery training centre and the other for engineers. These will shortly contain both active and reserve recruits who are arriving from basic training centres. No distinction is being made between them.
Present hutted accommodation is insufficient to take care of larger establishments. I might say that establishments of advanced centres have recently been increased. To avoid expense of constructing additional hutments, it has been decided for the summer to use canvas camps. These camps will be used by units whose present hutments are close to training centres, and hutments so released will be used for expansion of training centres. The reasons are, first, that training centres must be concentrated for administrative and training reasons, and, second, that units going into canvas camps may be moved in due course to other training areas or overseas.
I may say the hon. member mentioned that the camps were twelve miles from the present training camp. He is incorrectly informed with regard to that. I understand the camps are all within the camp area, and within a radius of about one mile from the centre of the hutted training camps.

There has been an extensive debate on this resolution providing for a tax of three cents a gallon on gasoline, and practically everything that could be said upon it has been said. I shall therefore be as brief as possible.
The farmers' side of the question has been very well presented, with perhaps one exception, and I should like to make this general observation with respect to the representatives in this house of the farmers of the west. I have heard several members ridicule members of this group who have made presentations on behalf of the farmer, the contention being that they had no right to speak for the farmer because they were not practical farmers themselves. I can see very little in that argument. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), for example, is not a fisherman; nevertheless he probably does a much better job of administering the Department of Fisheries than the average fisherman could do. The farmers of the west are to be congratulated upon the calibre of the men whom they have sent here to carry their message, and I am not confining that compliment to the members of any particular party but apply it to all those who have made representations on behalf of the farmers.
I view this proposal to tax the farmers in exactly the same light as I would view a similar situation affecting industrial workers. I view the present legislation and finding a solution for the problems of the farmers of western Canada in exactly the same light as I would view a situation where industrial workers were asked to reduce their time by fifty per cent, losing approximately fifty per cent of their earnings, and accepting a tax on their machinery of production. There is no difference between the two cases.
Some hon. members may wonder why no presentation is made on behalf of the farmers of Nova Scotia. It will help them to understand when I mention that a survey of farming conditions in Nova Scotia disclosed that in the period from 1901 to 1937, eighty per cent of the farms of Nova Scotia had become vacant, and this had been caused by people drifting away from the land and engaging in industry and other occupations because they were practically starving on the land. That

Special War Revenue Act
is not a good situation. One of the most essential steps for this government to take in any rehabilitation programme in the aftermath of this war would be to make a survey of the whole dominion with a view to laying down a well-planned agrarian programme. People in the last twenty years have pulled up their roots from the land and have become nomads wandering across the country searching for that elusive something which does not exist, namely, a job, and our job in the future ought to be to get the people back on the land where they really belong. The Minister of Finance and other ministers concerned could benefit by getting in touch with the extension department of Nova Scotia, which has inaugurated a programme with that end in view and has been studying it for the last few years as a partial solution of the problems of the people of that province, where, eighty per cent of the farms which were operating in 1901 are now vacant.
Where is it that eighty per cent of the farms are not now operating?

In Nova Scotia. That was shown by a survey of the period from 1901 to 1937.
I am, however, particularly interested in the fisherman and how this tax will affect him. The fisherman can very well be classed as the forgotten man. Our fishermen have really no one in this parliament to speak for them who understands their problem. I have interested myself in their problems to the extent of meeting with the fishermen in my constituency, and with all due respect to the Minister of Fisheries, who is doing his best to administer his department in the interests of the fishermen, no one can know the practical problem as it actually exists among the fishermen without being among them.
Unfortunately the Department of Fisheries has been crippled by a cutting-down of its estimates. Its estimates for 1940-41 were cut $150,000, which meant a considerable curtailment in the services rendered by the department in caring for the needs of the fishermen. Grants used to be made by the government to assist in the establishment of cold storage plants, and it was of great assistance to the fishermen to have proper storage facilities. That grant had to be eliminated because the appropriation for the Department of Fisheries was reduced. In addition, a twenty-three per cent cut was made in the inspection services. These inspectors moving round among the fishermen served a very good purpose in instructing them. The vote for fish culture was also reduced. The proper preparation of fish and the establishment of fish processing
plants was another service that had to be discontinued because the estimates of the department were reduced. The reduction may have been necessary on account of the war, but the curtailment of these services was a direct blow to the fishermen.
An examination of the earnings of the fishermen in the maritime provinces for 1940 shows-and this is set out in government statistics-that there were 40,000 fishermen and their gross earnings amounted to $879,000. Dividing that amount among 40,000 fishermen gives an income of about $220 a year to the fisherman.
Unemployment relief has also been discontinued. That is another blow to the fisherman. I think I am safe in saying that during the winter seventy-five per cent of the fishermen had to seek unemployment relief. That means of sustenance has gone from them. Indeed, the fishermen, of all classes of people in this dominion, have, I believe, suffered the most severe blows since the outbreak of the war. Everything that has happened has had a direct effect on their livelihood. They are not vocal. They have no one to speak for them, and as a result their story is not told. I hope the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), in his recruiting campaign, will take as many fishermen as possible from the maritime provinces, because I know it will be a welcome vocation to many of them to get into the army and have their needs taken care of for a short time.
This gasoline tax is an added burden on the fisherman. Since the outbreak of war they have experienced an increase in the cost of twine, rope, gear and everything else that they require to get out upon the water in the spring of the year. The cost of living has also risen to some extent. The fishermen are really in the pauper class; they have no income. This three per cent tax is now imposed on gasoline, which is the fuel they use in their fishing operations. Personally I am not particular how far the Minister of Finance goes in taxing gasoline that is used for pleasure purposes, but I wish to add my voice to those we have already heard on behalf of that forgotten class of people, the fishermen. The Minister of Finance would be well advised if he considered some alternative tax. I do not see any revenue in this tax for him anyway so far as the fishermen are concerned, because it will be an added burden on that class of people and will mean that they will not be able to go out and pursue their calling. As I said, government statistics show that the average income of the fisherman is $220 a year. In addition, the cost of living
Special War Revenue Act

and the cost of gear have increased, and there is always the hazard of losing that gear in storms. Conditions generally are such that the fisherman will not be able much longer to continue in his calling. Many of the reductions in the votes of the Department of Fisheries, while it may have been necessary to reduce expenditure on account of the war, might very well be reexamined, and some of the votes certainly should be restored.
In addition to that, I do not think any other group of people in Canada have made greater efforts to do something for themselves. For the past two or three years the fishermen have tried to organize, form cooperative groups, educate one another, and promote markets; and they have gone a long way in that direction. Instead of the grants for the cold storage plant, the fish processing plant and the educational activities which they are carrying on, being discontinued, they should be continued. I suggest that the Minister of Finance make a reexamination of this matter.

It is the undoubted duty of the Chairman or of Mr. Speaker to maintain the rules of the house in debate. The rules of the house have been adopted as a result of the experience and wisdom of parliament. Many of our rules have come down to us as a result of the experience of the mother of parliaments, the British parliament, to carry on in an orderly and practical way the proceedings of parliament; and without these rules there is no doubt that our proceedings would fall into contempt, not only as regards hon. members, but in the minds of the public as well.
Standing order 58 is well known. I have had occasion several times to draw the attention of hon. members to it. It reads, in part:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
In the debates on the address and on the budget great latitude has always been allowed to hon. members to discuss the principles involved in the speech from the throne or in the budget speech. When, however, that stage has been passed, when we have reached the committee stage, we are governed by standing order 58, and particularly by subsection 2, and I draw the attention of hon. members to the word "strictly" which is therein used. That means that there is very little latitude. The rule must be interpreted in a restrictive way, and a discussion in committee should be strictly relevant to the item under discussion.
It is at present proposed to impose a tax of three cents a gallon on gasoline. General discussion of principle as to the effect of this legislation on this, that or the other class of Canadian citizens is not, in my opinion, strictly relevant to the item now before the committee.
What would be relevant?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is too wide. I must maintain that the point of order is well taken. Hon. members should discuss this item; their remarks should be strictly relevant.
I had just about finished, anyway. I realize that the Minister of Finance is probably right.

You got on Hansard what you wanted to say, though, did you not?

Special War Revenue Act
Certainly. Last night I listened to a fellow roaming round here with a horse and buggy, back a hundred years ago, and no objection was taken to that.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am merely trying to point out that a particular group that will be affected by this tax are not in a position to pay it, and that if the trend in the direction of curtailment of moneys necessary to keep these people in employment is continued much longer, there will be no revenue from this particular group and they will be unemployed one hundred per cent. That was what I tried to make clear, and in order to do that, I must of necessity talk about the economic conditions of these people as related to legislation which has recently gone through the house. I trust that someone else will take up the case of the fishermen, make an examination of it, and see if we cannot give them a little more attention in this parliament.

Last evening, when this item was first called, I at once lodged a protest. My remarks were brief because I was trying to' facilitate these proceedings, but I pointed out as concisely as I could that this tax would impose a hardship on producers, particularly in western Canada. I could have gone, as many did, into great detail. During the discussion I listened to a good many arguments, which seemed to me sound, in opposition to this tax on the producer, and I also heard a suggestion that producers should be granted an exemption or a rebate of some kind. In the minister's many replies I was unable to find any really sound objections to the suggestions which were made; indeed, I thought he admitted that a certain amount of hardship would be enacted if this tax goes through. He pointed out that this tax is first of all on the refinery. In that respect it seems to me that an injustice is being done. In western Canada some cooperative refineries have started up. One I have in mind, the Consumers' Refinery, in Regina, began operations in the last year or two under great difficulties. They are doing an important work in distributing gasoline direct to producers within a radius of many miles of Regina.
The minister also suggested that there were certain difficulties of administration in connection with either a rebate or an exemption, and I must say that I was not impressed with his arguments in that regard. As to the system in Saskatchewan and Alberta, I do not think that if it were employed, and if coloured
gas were used as indicated, there would be any great difficulty. The minister spoke about certain prosecutions-over 201. I suggest that if a severe penalty were imposed, such as there is in Saskatchewan, it would meet the difficulty. Where it was found that coloured gas was illegally used, they could suspend the use of the offender's car for a month, and no man would take the chance, for the sake of three cents a gallon on eight or ten gallons of gasoline, of having his car impounded. I do not see why the difficulties could not be overcome.
I think the great majority of hon. members last night were opposed to this tax being imposed at the present time, and if a vote had been taken I believe that the opposition would have carried. In order to be brief and to bring the matter to a point, I move the following amendment:
That resolution 6 of the Special War Revenue Act be amended by adding thereto the following words:
Provided, however, that a rebate of the full amount of the tax paid by any farmer or fisherman shall be made upon satisfactory proof that the gasoline upon which the tax was paid was utilized by such farmer or fisherman exclusively for power purposes upon his farm or in his fishing boat.
That amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I have no doubt that the minister's staff could carry it out so as to exempt from the tax the producers indicated in the amendment. I do not think there would be any difficulty. I could mention many directions in which the staffs of different departments are employed, and money is spent, to do work and to get information in connection with matters of little or no consequence. There is no reason, therefore, why the staff of the department could not cany out this amendment.
Reference has been made to the nationalization of the whole industry. In this connection, I would point out that in western Canada, in Saskatchewan and Alberta, there is a great deposit of tar sands which, if properly developed, would pay the whole cost of the war. There we have a natural resource, and a formula for extracting or refining gas from tar sands has been discovered which would make the project quite feasible. Gas could be produced cheaply and could be delivered in the city of Regina at nine cents a gallon. Towards Hudson bay there is a natural supply which could be reached by pipeline, and it would provide gas at a considerably reduced rate.
Special War Revenue Act

I have no objection to
giving rebates to farmers and fishermen; far from it. In fact, I have supported that kind of legislation for bonuses, subventions, subsidies, rebates and so forth. Surely, however, in the name of all fairness, some consideration should be given to the industrial workers in our cities, who constitute nearly forty-two per cent of our population and live eight, ten or fifteen miles from the city and the munitions plants. They are obliged to walk considerable distances when the street cars are not running. If the principle of this amendment is to apply at all, it should be made to apply to the industrial workers who are engaged in the manufacture of munitions, working on three shifts. I repeat, many of them have to walk miles in the middle of the night. Why should they not be considered?
We have dealt generously in this parliament with farmers and fishermen. Take, for example, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. In 1935 I urged that the principle of that act should be extended to take in the industrial workers. Soldiers should not pay this three-cent tax on gasoline, I do not know where this process is going to stop. If this rebate is made we might as well abolish the whole revenue bill. I understand that no amendment to a revenue bill can be moved involving discrimination between one class of taxpayers and another, unless the minister consents. How does the minister expect the munition workers in Mimico, Brampton, Richmond Hill, Newmarket, Scarboro and other centres, who are engaged in the manufacture of all kinds of munitions, to carry on and discharge their duties effectively if they are discriminated against? Many of them are farmers who do not wish to work any longer on farms, when they can get forty-five or fifty cents an hour making munitions. I appeal for common justice for our industrial workers, urban and suburban, in connection with this tax. I think the amendment is out of order, and in any event, unless the principle is extended as I suggest, I will oppose it. We have had enough of bonuses, exemptions and subsidies, discriminating between different classes of taxpayers and against soldiers and industrial workers.

As seconder of the
amendment I wish to add a word to what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) has said. In the first place, with reference to the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member for Fort William, who advocate the horse-and-buggy system-

No; it is a team in a
horse-buggy.

Sometimes they use
the team and the buggy too. A few years ago, officials of the federal department made a survey of the prairie provinces iff order to find out the cost of producing a bushel of wheat. The survey was carried out on a yield considerably higher than the average for the past twelve years, and the finding was that it cost, to produce one bushel on a quarter-section, with a man and four horses, $1.02, whereas with a tractor and power equipment on a two-section farm the cost was fifty-four cents. Even that does not reimburse the producer for the cost of production as intimated by the Minister of Agriculture during the past few months.
In the last few years the number of tenant farmers has increased not only in the prairie provinces but throughout the country. As was pointed out last night, many of those whose parents had owned their farms have lost ownership in recent years, and that condition is on the increase. The disparity has been greatly enhanced by the present government, in some instances by order in council. I am referring to the disparity that exists to-day between industry and organized labour on the one hand and the agricultural population on the other, even without this added tax on gas. Like many others, I am heartily in accord with the suggestion that gas for pleasure purposes should be taxed. I advocated this myself when the budget was under discussion a year ago; and I cannot see why, under a system of proper cooperation with the provincial government, the collection of the gasoline tax could not be handled for the federal government and the necessary rebates for agricultural producers put into force.
The previous speaker made some reference to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, but the people of Manitoba do not enjoy the benefits of that act at the present time, and with the present prospects for agriculture they are going to be in a veiy serious position this year. I implore the minister to do something about refunding this tax. I am satisfied that a majority of the members of this house, not only .those of the opposition but those on the government side as well, are opposed to this tax on gasoline used for agricultural purposes, and I trust that they will do their duty as private members in voting on this amendment.

I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without adding my voice to those who have already expressed themselves as being in favour of a refund of the tax paid on gasoline used by farmers and fishermen in the conduct of their business. One of the main

Special War Revenue Act
reasons mentioned by the minister for not making this refund was the difficulty that might be experienced in connection with administration. Well, already the provinces are administering similar legislation, and while there might be some difficulties I believe many of them could be ironed out by cooperation with the provinces and by accepting their methods of granting refunds.
The minister says that refunds in such cases would make the whole scheme very difficult to administer. That may be so, but already the minister has imposed taxes that are equally difficult to administer. I have particular reference to the national defence tax as it relates to farm labour. All farm labour is subject to the national defence tax if the rate of pay is equivalent to a certain sum per year. I should think that would be far more difficult to administer fairly than these refunds possibly could be, because the majority of the farmers of this country are not making returns in connection with their periodical or day labour. If in one case the minister does not hesitate to impose a tax that may be hard to administer, he should not fear the difficulties that may be experienced in connection with refunds on gasoline used by farmers and fishermen.
I am sorry that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle did not go a little further. In this province, and I think in other parts of the country, we have what is known as custom threshing, carried on by men who own and operate threshing machines using gasoline or crude oil. The man operating a machine that uses crude oil will pay no tax whatever, while the man operating a machine using gasoline will have to pay this tax. Thus one man will be placed in a very unfair position in relation to the other, and a matter of that kind is very difficult to adjust because it is almost impossible to change most tractors from one fuel to the other. A tractor built and . equipped for the use of gasoline can hardly be changed over to use crude oil, certainly not without considerable expense. Therefore the thresher who is using gasoline will find himself at a distinct disadvantage. The minister might consider this point also.
I rose merely for the purpose of expressing my full agreement with the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I appeal to the minister once more to adjust this tax, because after all it will add considerably to the cost of production on the farm, and if there is one thing we need to watch to-day more than another it is the cost of production.

In rising to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle I do not plan to review the present position of agriculture in Canada. When the minister delivered his budget address he announced that the provision exempting from income tax all interest payable in currency other than Canadian funds would be repealed. Before a single protest was made in this house, however, the minister announced a change which he said would cost the treasury between eight and ten million dollars in revenue. In explaining the reason for this change the minister said, as reported at page 2878 of Hansard:
After I heart! a number of these representations, many by gentlemen who were most considerate, most friendly, and who appeared to be as anxious as we are to advance the war effort of Canada, I was convinced that it would be injurious to the credit of Canada if we continued that provision.
I do not intend to review the discussion that has taken place in that regard, but I want to point out that the minister listened to people outside of this house, to the extent of relieving them of a burden of from eight to ten million dollars. Hon. members in all parts of this house have taken exception to this tax on gasoline as applied to farmers and fishermen, which will take money from the pockets of Canadians who cannot afford to pay it. I am sure hon. members have received a great many protests in this connection, of which perhaps this is typical:
Most farmers are obliged to use high test fuel in their tractors, and thus have to pay the tax, which greatly depreciates farm income. We even pay this tax in order to get the summer-fallow bonus. This seems a misplacement of burden to us in this locality, as we farmers feel we already are carrying the major part of this war burden.
This is a mild statement of the predicament in which Canadian farmers find themselves. I do not believe many people in the country will take seriously the remarks of the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member for Fort William, but I am very glad only two hon. members of this entire house are in favour of going back to the horse and buggy days. When our electric lights failed a short time ago and this chamber was lighted by the equivalent of about one candle power, it occurred to me that very few hon. members would seriously suggest that we should return to the days of candles and horses and oxen.
The hon. member for Brant talked a lot of good horse sense all the same.

Perhaps, from the point of view of the hon. member who has just spoken; and perhaps that means that we have
Special War Revenue Act

three members of this house who hold the view expressed by the hon. member for Brant. This year we are being asked to appropriate over $13,000,000 for the ordinary activities of the Department of Agriculture, without taking into consideration the $35,000,000 bonus and other special grants. Surely in this day and age no one is going to suggest that we should ignore the findings of those who have carried on investigations into various aspects of agriculture during all these years. I hope the minister will extend to hon. members of this house the courtesy he has shown already to people outside the house, who have been able to relieve their friends of from eight to ten million dollars in taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This discussion is proceeding as though the amendment were quite in order, and I think perhaps that matter had better be cleared up at the outset. If I remember correctly the hon. member for Qu'Appelle moved a similar amendment last year in regard to another tax, and at that time his amendment was ruled out of order on the grounds on which I suggest this amendment is not in order now. Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, paragraph 552, at page 164, reads:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
It is an essential part of the financial scheme submitted by the government that we impose taxes intended to yield $300,000,000, of which $25,000,000, it is estimated, will be derived from the gasoline tax. The proposal to pay refunds or to make rebates on this amount will substantially diminish the receipts; I do not know just to what extent. I believe the figures show that the provinces pay back about one-sixth of the amount collected on gasoline. That is, about five-sixths of gasoline sales are taxable. If that proportion held in this instance it would mean a diminution of our revenues, and a curtailment of the financial scheme submitted by the government, to the extent of between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000. Therefore I submit the amendment is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does any other hon. member wish to speak to the point of order?
If anything is done, will the minister include returned soldiers?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question now before the committee is a point of order, and that is the only matter which may now be debated. Does any other hon. member wish to speak? If not, I shall proceed to give my ruling.
The amendment is to the effect that there shall be. a rebate of the full amount of the tax paid by any farmer or fisherman, upon proof that the gasoline upon which the tax was paid was utilized by such farmer or fisherman exclusively for power purposes upon his farm or in his fishing boat.
There is not the slightest doubt that the effect of the amendment would be considerably to reduce the revenue to be derived from the scheme of legislation now submitted to the committee. Therefore such an amendment would detrimentally affect the balance of ways and means to be voted for the service for the present year. For these reasons I must declare the amendment out of order. My ruling is in keeping with rulings made in the past in respect of similar motions.
Apparently the minister has adopted a defeatist attitude on this question.
Just the opposite.

He has said, and in the past the Prime Minister has emphasized, that during the war we should do everything possible to maintain the principle of equality of sacrifice. Apparently the minister has considered it desirable, if possible, to exempt farmers and fishermen from this tax, but he says he has not been able to devise any means by which this may be brought about.
The purpose of the tax is twofold: the conservation of foreign exchange by reducing gasoline sales, and the raising of revenue. I should like to deal with the first of those two purposes. To what extent will the application of this tax on gasoline used on the farm reduce consumption of gasoline by farmers? I am satisfied it will have little or no effect. Once a farm becomes mechanized and is being run efficiently, in order to reduce costs the farmer will use as little gasoline as possible. But even though the price of gasoline be increased, he will have to use it in order to operate his machinery. Therefore the placing of a tax on gasoline used by the farmer will not affect materially its consumption.
I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood). I do not think his

Special War Revenue Act
arguments are sound when he is speaking about farming operations in western Canada, but as a rule they are amusing. He suggested that some hon. members on this side of the house should keep both feet on the ground. I suggest that his feet are below the ground, and he is completely bogged down. The hon. member may be competent to discuss questions of agriculture in eastern Canada, because I believe he has farmed in this part of the country, but his arguments prove conclusively that he understands very little about agriculture in western Canada. I have farmed in western Canada for over thirty years, and therefore I feel justified in making one or two comments in reply to the arguments raised yesterday by the hon. member.
He suggested that farmers should dispense with tractors, go back to the use of horses, and thereby eliminate consumption of gasoline and avoid any payment of gasoline tax. He has suggested that the financial plight of farmers in western Canada is due largely to the purchase of tractors. But if he will go into the wheat belt of western Canada he will invariably find that the best farmers are tractor farmers, while the poorest farmers, speaking financially, are horse farmers. This seems to prove conclusively that his argument does not hold water.
Why has western Canada become mechanized? The hon. member has tried to show that the mechanization of the west has brought about the financial difficulties of the farmers. Western Canada has become mechanized so as to make it possible for the farmers to produce wheat at the low prices they have had to accept. When the price of wheat is reduced, then the only way to produce wheat at the reduced figure is to increase the size of operations. To do that one must farm on a larger scale and spread the overhead over a larger number of acres. It has been the policy of this government from 1935 to 1939, that of allowing the price of wheat to fall below a proper level, which has brought about an extension of the large mechanized units. Whether or not the government intended that that should be the result, its policy has had the effect of driving the small farmer off his farm. The small farms are being taken over by mortgage companies and are being incorporated in large mechanized units. I do not say that that is the object that the government has had in view, but that has been the result of its policy. I do not think anyone would suggest for one moment that it is a desirable condition.
I wonder if the hon. member for Brant really thought out the facts when he said 14873-191
yesterday that the farmers of western Canada should go back to the use of horses. If his proposal were adopted, what would be the result in respect of the large mechanized units? Those large farms do not have horses at all, so that they would have to purchase horses. They have no bams, so that they would have to build barns. They have no harness, so that they would have to buy harness. They have no horse-drawn machinery, so that they would have to buy horse-drawn machinery. It is obvious that his suggestion would bring about a tremendous expenditure of capital. Would that be advantageous to Canada's war effort? If the farmers were to go back to farming with the use of horses, what would be the result in respect of the labour situation? A tremendous number of men would be needed to operate those farms. Would that help the war effort? Would it be advantageous to our war effort to take men away from industry and place them on farms, or to take men who might enlist and place them on farms? Yet that would undoubtedly be the result. The combine has displaced a tremendous amount of man-power. Take away the combines and go back to the old type of farming and threshing and you will again need your harvest trains to transport men to western Canada.

At present there is an overabundance of wheat and we are asking Canadian citizens to pay for something they do not want. There are 500,000,000 bushels stored in the elevators in the west. There is no sale for this wheat, and yet you are asking the taxpayers for more money with which to grow more of a commodity which they do not want.

But that condition has
been brought about by the government's policy. Had the government adopted the policy which we have advocated in this house year after year, 'that condition would not have arisen. We have advocated a guaranteed increased price for limited deliveries of wheat. Just as long as the farmer may sell all the wheat he produces even at a low price, he will have to increase his operations in order to reduce his overhead.

And aggravate a situation
which is already bad.
As a result of the government's policy. If you have a guaranteed price on limited deliveries, that situation will not occur.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We had more wheat in 1928 than we have had since.

Special War Revenue Act

Deliveries were not
restricted then to 1,500 bushels; the price was at a low figure and deliveries of 5,000 bushels could be made. Mr. Chairman, if I am out of order I have been drawn into that position by certain questions which have been asked.
The second reason for introducing this tax is the necessity for raising revenue. Will the minister dare say that this tax carries out the principle which he laid1 down on a former occasion when he stated that taxation should be imposed upon the basis of equality of sacrifice having regard to the ability to pay? The minister knows very well that this tax absolutely contravenes that principle. If he has any doubt, I suggest that he get in touch with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and have him repeat what he has said to the farmers of western Canada. The Minister of Agriculture said this:
They know that this policy is taking money out of their pockets and making it possible for this dominion to finance the war to the extent of at least $100,000,000 more than would be the case if the government did for the wheat growers of the west what they are doing for most of the other people of Canada.
I wonder if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will agree with that statement. If he does, then he must admit that this tax does not carry out the principle which he has laid down on eveiy occasion on which he has discussed the financial policy of this dominion. Speaking throughout .the country the Minister of Agriculture has stated that he realized that the farmers of the west were not getting a square deal. He criticized the high prices of farm machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Any time I have referred to farmers, it has been .the farmers of Canada.

This tax means more to western Canada because it is there that you have the large mechanized units. I was referring to the prices of farm machinery. The Minister of Agriculture objected to these high prices, but the only excuse that he could present .to the farmers was that he was simply one of a cabinet of sixteen and therefore was not able to do anything about it. Instead of saying that, I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that now is the time to protest in this house while these matters are being discussed, If the Minister of Agriculture were to rise in his place and criticize this tax it might have a beneficial effect upon some of the other Liberal members from western Canada. I have not heard one Liberal member from Alberta rise in his place and protest against this tax. If the Minister of Agriculture would lead the way I am satisfied that other members would have the courage to criticize this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am leaving the discussion of that question until I am on my estimates, when I think I would be more in order. A number of hon. members from that corner have referred to my opinion as to the use of horses or gasoline in farming. I should like to say that I have a farm in western Canada and I have never had a tractor.

The Minister of Agriculture is not dependent upon his farm for a living; he has quite a substantial income as a minister and a member of parliament. If he were dependent upon his farm for a living he would be broke by now.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If I were dependent upon my farm for a living, as I have been at times, I certainly would not use a tractor.
The minister is apparently admitting that his farm is not suitable for a tractor; therefore his argument is not relevant.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is a pretty good farm, just about the average for western Canada.
That might be a matter of opinion.
Can the minister raise wheat for 38 cents a bushel with horses?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us come back to the gasoline tax.
Practically every member who has spoken has been opposed to this tax. I believe that every hon. member who truly represented the feelings of his constituency would be opposed to it.
What is the provincial tax in Alberta?
Seven cents per gallon.
In the light of the fact that we are at war, could not the hon. member, as a citizen of Alberta, persuade the government of that province to reduce the provincial tax on gasoline?

The provincial government recognizes the fact that the farmers are not in position to pay that tax, and they are exempt. We use a coloured gasoline to carry out that exemption. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if the provinces can find ways and means of exempting the farmers from the gasoline tax, the dominion government should be just as competent to deal with the matter.
I was pointing out that I believe that the majority of hon. members, if they truly represented the will of their electors, would oppose this tax. But we all know that the tax will

Special War Revenue Act
go through in its present form. It is not a pleasant reflection upon what we call democracy when we realize that that will happen. We hear a great deal about democracy and how we are fighting dictatorships, yet in this country we have nothing more or less than a financial dictatorship. This is the dictatorship which sabotaged the industry of this country before the war. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) suggested the other day, this is the dictatorship which has the brake firmly clamped down upon our war effort to-day. This is the dictatorship which has sabotaged agriculture to a point where the small farmer will be driven off his farm and absorbed by the mortgage companies. We all know that the plight of agriculture is tragic. Debts are being built up which will never be paid. I say in all seriousness that the work being done now through the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the other boards will have to be done all over again. There is a very serious problem which will have to be faced in the future. This is not a problem which can be solved by a large colonization scheme after the war, under which the mortgage companies which have taken over these farms will sell them to immigrants and turn our farmers off the land. We must still face the problem of what to do with the men who still have farms but who have gone broke.
The minister has suggested that this revenue must be raised and that we have offered no alternatives. When I spoke on the resolution having to do with the ten per cent tax on railway fares I pointed out that the minister was missing one very good source of taxation by not taxing advertising in the press and various periodicals as well as over the radio. For instance, a tax could be imposed on the soap programmes, the quiz programmes, and many others. There is a source of revenue which might very well be tapped by the minister and which would make it unnecessary to impose this particular tax.
I have on several occasions pointed out that we do not object to reasonable taxation so long as it is imposed upon the people in the most equitable way, but we feel that once we have placed upon the people as great an amount of taxation as we think they can bear, the logical thing from that point on is to utilize the services of the Bank of Canada. I have not yet heard from the minister one sound argument why that should not be done. He did make the excuse that as the result of such an operation there would be inflation on the part of the chartered banks. But that could be overcome by compelling the chartered banks to increase their cash 14873-1914
reserves. I have never yet heard the minister answer why that could not be done. In this way we could impose reasonable taxation without going down into places where great hardship and injustice will be done, as will be the case with regard to this particular tax.

I listened to what the
Minister of Finance said yesterday with reference to the gasoline tax. He impressed me definitely with the idea that he felt this tax should not be imposed on agriculture and fishing and that the only reason why he was not in favour of a rebate of the tax for agriculture and fishing was the difficulty of administration. This bears out what I said in my last speech in this house. I stated that the minister got from administrative officials only his information about the difficulties of administration and abuses where different systems of rebate are in operation. But from my knowledge of how the purple gas system works in Saskatchewan, and having spoken to the people administering the system in the province, knowing also how successful it is, I say, and I think every member from Saskatchewan who says exactly what he thinks will say the same, that there are no wholesale evasions of the tax in Saskatchewan such as the minister mentioned and such as his administrative officials suggested. Actually the act which provides for the sale of purple gas to farmers for agricultural purposes only is working extremely well. Saskatchewan did have a system providing for the sale of gasoline to farmers and providing for application for rebates in connection therewith. It was suggested, however, that if a specially treated gas were sold to farmers for agricultural purposes it would save the long delay in the farmers getting the rebate and might lead to fewer evasions of the act by making claims where gas is not used for agricultural purposes. There were many who doubted the wisdom of introducing this system of purple gas, but what has happened, to the knowledge of almost every member from Saskatchewan, is that the purple gas system has worked better than the system of rebates, and more money is realized than when the system of rebates was in force. Without any increase in the number of inspectors the act is being successfully enforced. It is true that since the act came into operation over two years ago there has been an average of thirty prosecutions a month, but I understand that these prosecutions are getting fewer because it is being brought home to everyone that the tax cannot be successfully evaded. There is no question about that; all you have to do is ask any person from Saskatchewan who knows anything about it.
Special War Revenue Act

What does happen is this. If a very little bit of that purple gas is left in the tank and the tank is then filled up with regular gas, an inspector can tell right away that at one time there was purple gas in the tank. Some persons have found this out to their cost, and when a few of them are caught, it soon becomes known that you cannot get away with any attempt at evasion of the tax. The purple gas system is pretty well accepted now in Saskatchewan as being better than the refund system, and the provincial government is maintaining it because it finds that it works. It certainly would not maintain it, not for one minute, if there were wholesale evasions. Actually in this regard the situation is improving day by day.
That being so, Mr. Chairman, I come to the point I raised in my last speech in this house, that if hon. members were consulted instead of departmental officials, who I am afraid in some cases are more concerned about getting a tax that is easy to administer than one that is fair to the people as a whole, a different attitude might be taken. I have been very much perturbed over this situation. Coming as I do from Saskatchewan, where, to the knowledge of every member from Saskatchewan, the system of the sale of purple gas to farmers works excellently, I am told on the floor of this house by the Minister of Finance that while he realizes that his proposed gasoline tax should not be imposed on the agricultural industry, it is being adhered to because of the difficulties of administration in an alternative system, that his administrative officials tell him something which I myself, so far as any one can know anything, know to be not so. If then I do not stand up in this house and tell hon. members exactly what I know to be the facts I am abdicating my position, Mr. Chairman, in favour of these departmental officials. I cannot see it in any other way. Finding myself in this position, and knowing how necessary it is for the government to raise money-I do not for a moment wish to embarrass the government- I then have to ask myself what I should do. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) said last night, and he was not contradicted by the government, that a motion in respect to this matter would not be a motion of want of confidence in the government, that it would be merely giving expression to what we think about the tax. After very anxious consideration, therefore, I have decided to move an amendment. It is the first time I have done this as a member of the house, and I shall tell the house, after moving the amendment, why I felt I could not do otherwise.

I propose, seconded by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Turner), to move the following amendment:
That resolution 6 of the Special War Revenue Act be amended by striking out the word "three" wherever it occurs therein and replacing it by the word "four" and by adding thereto the following words:
"Provided that gasoline referred to herein shall not be presumed to include power fuel sold in any province solely for and limited by the law of such province to agricultural or fishing purposes."
In the first place I do not think anyone will deny that the people who use gasoline for pleasure purposes can much more easily afford to pay four cents than agriculturists and fishermen can afford to pay three. Therefore I do not think anyone will argue as to the equity of my proposal. In fact the Minister of Finance himself said that he had thought of imposing a tax of five cents. I have suggested that the tax be increased only by sufficient to make up for the diminution in revenue by exempting gasoline used for agricultural and fishing purposes.
It may be said that we have not that system in every province. My answer to that is this: you are not imposing a tax on diesel fuel or on distillates. You could very well, then, exempt fuel which is used solely for power purposes in connection with agriculture and fisheries. There is no change in the principle.
In regard to the question of administration, I grant that there should be uniformity throughout the country, but I am satisfied that if the law in the form proposed passed this parliament, the coming into force of the provision could be suspended until a conference was held between all the provinces, as a result of which they would probably agree to impose this system of putting out, under the law of the province, a special coloured fuel for agricultural purposes; and when that was done, this provision could be brought into effect. All the provinces are interested in seeing to it that no gasoline shall be used without a tax for purposes other than agriculture and fisheries because otherwise they lose revenue. In other words there is, as far as this government is concerned, no problem of administration. All it has to do is simply to say, we do not tax diesel fuel, distillates, and power fuel which by the law of the province can be used only for power purposes; and as every province of Canada, I believe, exempts this class of fuel, every province will see to it that the law is enforced.

Diesel fuel is not mentioned in this resolution.

Special War Revenue Act

I know; there is no tax on it, and there is no tax on distillate, but I am just saying that the tax should not apply to power fuel.
I was born in western Canada; I was brought up there and have spent my whole life there. I have seen what has been happening to agriculture in the west, particularly in Saskatchewan. I am not going to discuss what I have seen, but it makes me feel that a further tax upon the farming industry in western Canada, and particularly in my own province, will not be a good thing for Canada.
I say advisedly that in the long run it will have as grave an effect upon the unity of the country as anything else which has happened in the last ten years. The feeling out there is that they have been driven to the limit of their endurance, and if a further tax such as the one proposed is put upon them, the results will not be pleasant to contemplate. If that is only my opinion, at all events it is the opinion of one whose father was born in Canada, who himself was born in the west, and who feels it his duty to his conscience and to his country to warn the minister not to insist upon putting this impost on an industry which has been driven almost beyond the limits of endurance.
I do not need to go into the present position of the farmers, especially in Saskatchewan. I do not need to point out the effect which an additional tax will have upon the ability of our farmers to provide their children with educational facilities. I do not need to emphasize the consequences in the matter of their getting hospital and medical facilities for their children. Certainly it is not necessary to point out any of these things to this committee, because they are familiar with the report of the Sirois commission, which states that unless something is done we shall have in this country "second-class" citizens who cannot afford for their children things which are available to people in other parts of the dominion; and that condition is not being remedied through this war, although an impartial commission, upon which not a single Saskatchewan representative sat, made this solemn finding. In other words, you are condemning some of our people to be second-class citizens, and if there is anything we condemn overseas, it is that hellish doctrine of Hitler's that there shall be a master people and a second-class or servile people. We cannot rationally condemn-I say this with all earnestness-the practices against which we are going to fight to our last drop of blood, and condone anything approaching these practices at home. We ourselves may
not say anything along this line, but people will be found to go out and tell the farmers what is happening to them and what is being done by the government of this country.
This tax cannot be passed on by the agriculturists. The prices of everything they have to sell are fixed by government boards or by agreements, and in the case of practically our only purchaser, Great Britain, they are fixed fairly rigidly, excepting possibly as regards bacon. Now, when we place a tax upon a labouring man, for example, a railway man, and so increase his cost of living, we immediately give him the right to apply to have his wages raised in order to take care of that increased cost of living. In all earnestness I ask every hon. member, and I ask the labour representatives particularly-
Mr. MacNIC'OL: There aren't any.

-I ask every hon. member: can you condone a system which protects labour from increases in the cost of living due to the rise in taxes, and put further taxes upon the agricultural industry, which cannot pass on its costs and which to-day is down to the minimum standard of living?
I assure my colleagues of the party to which I belong that I take this position with some regret, but I do it, Mr. Chairman, because I feel that the people who trust me to come here and speak for them would not have me do other than I have done. When some hon. members say they have received no protests against this tax from their constituencies, may I observe that, for my own part, I like to think that my constituents have enough confidence in my devotion to their interests not to think it necessary continually to write and advise me as to what I should do, or to remind me of my bounden duty. They are, perhaps, sitting at home, feeling and knowing that this government will do what it feels to be the very best it can under the circumstances-I am sure that is what the government is doing-and convinced that the government will not impose any tax beyond what it is impossible to avoid, because, they will say, "The government must know we cannot afford to bear it". Therefore they rely upon us to see to it that a tax of this kind shall not be laid upon our farmers and fishermen if it can possibly be avoided.
I believe I have shown a way by which this exemption can be granted without any diminution of the revenues required by this country to prosecute the war. I believe I have shown the Minister of Finance-and by the look of him I fear I have not convinced him-one way of avoiding this tax. I believe he will admit that he does not desire to put any further burdens upon the classes of citizen of
Special War Revenue Act

whom I have spoken. If there is any possibility of making this scheme work which I have proposed, it is worthy of further consideration; above all, it is worthy of a hurried consultation with, at least, some of the members of the provincial governments, to find out whether the wholesale evasions which the minister fears would in fact take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am certainly not prepared to answer such an impassioned and also reasoned speech as that which my hon. friend the member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has just delivered. As I said last night, this matter was given serious consideration and two alternatives were discussed. One was that a considerably higher tax on gasoline should be imposed which would apply to the general public, with a system of refunds or rebates to farmers, fishermen and tourists. The plan we had in mind would have yielded a great deal more money than this plan, and, as I said last night, after considerable investigation and discussion of the matter, not only with officials of the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue but with members of governments-not of all governments- persons who had been members of governments, and others who are pretty well acquainted with the abuses and evasions in the provinces, which, as the hon. gentleman himself admits, have led to an average of thirty prosecutions a month in Saskatchewan in the last two years, it was decided that we could not afford to put the dominion government into this type of business. It has been said to me on more than one occasion-at least on one occasion-that if those engaged in provincial politics had the thing to do over again they would at all costs avoid refunds.
Apparently the members of the house who have spoken regard it as an unimportant consideration that the government of Canada should tax cleanly and effectively and that when it imposes taxes it should collect them. I cannot regard that as unimportant; I think it is one of the most important considerations. After full study, therefore, it was decided that we would modify the tax, that we would reduce it to three cents. While it will affect numbers of people in Canada who cannot very well afford to pay it, at the same time we are imposing a great many taxes on people who cannot afford to pay them, in the sense that they cannot afford to do so without sacrifice. We did think that the farming and fishing communities, under the very grave circumstances of the hour, would not protest, would not take violent exception to the tax. I am perhaps inclined to be led into the introduction of

considerations that are not strictly relevant, but hon. gentlemen must realize the tremendous gravity of this hour. They must realize that the government of Canada is doing things which it would not think of doing under normal conditions.
I thought that certain members, including the hon. member who has just spoken, would sooner or later make exactly the type of speech which he has made. It does not surprise me a bit, because he made just about the same type of speech last year in connection with the war exchange tax. I do not blame him altogether, but he places a loyalty to the financial dollar and cent interests of his constituents above practically every other earthly consideration.

I rise to a point of order. That is absolutely uncalled for. I am suggesting that we raise the same amount of money or more by another means which will be fairer, and as a person who in the last war, as soon as he was eighteen, got into the army and went to France to serve his country even at the risk of his life, I resent most fiercely the suggestion that I put loyalty to my constituents' financial interests above loyalty to my country. I ask the minister to withdraw that suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is asking me to withdraw the suggestion that he placed such a consideration above loyalty to his country, I withdraw it; and perhaps the words "earthly consideration" were a little too wide. There are, however, times and circumstances in which this violent plea not to touch people at all under conditions like these is a little bit out of place. As everyone knows, it is not an easy thing to finance this war. I had to sit through a debate here the other night, and I did not altogether blame members for making the speeches they did. We have placed a national defence tax on girls and boys, on men and women who are earning as little as $660 a year, which is only $55 a month. There was a considerable protest about that from all parts of the house. If, however, we are to be driven out of all taxes that cause sacrifice, we are not going to be able to finance the war except in the way suggested by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who says we should do it by creating money, printing money. He says, "call in the services of the Bank of Canada," which means printing money.

Only to the extent that the government cannot raise the required revenue from reasonable taxation and sale of war savings certificates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know what the committee wants to do with this resolution. I did not correct an hon. gentleman last night when he said it would not be a vote of want, of confidence in the government, but I may tell the House of Commons that the government has seriously considered these various proposals and has come to the conclusion that, nevertheless, realizing what it is doing, it has to ask the Canadian people to assume this burden. As I have said before, the general public expected that we would increase the sales tax, but we have refrained from doing so. On every occasion, with the possible exception of the war exchange tax, when imposing taxes we have refrained from making levies which would affect the agricultural portion of the community; and no tax we have imposed has borne with particular weight upon that section of the population. It is simply that they pay what happens to light upon them as part of the general body politic. I cannot make my record one hundred per cent perfect of not imposing taxes that will to some degree be borne by farmers. I cannot do that and get ahead with the financial programme of the government.
I believe that this three-cent tax, which is very small in proportion to the tax that we originally intended to suggest to the House of Commons, the agricultural community of Canada generally will be prepared to assume. A great many farmers in the west will not be paying tax on power because they will be using in their tractors a type of fuel which is not taxable. Some of them will be paying this tax. I do not think, however, that at a time like this that fact justified the impassioned and violent type of speech which we have heard from the hon. member for Rosthern.
Is the minister aware that the majority of tractors used in western Canada are high-powered tractors which must use gasoline? The diesel form of tractor is very rare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have had conflicting reports and conflicting stories about the proportion that must use gasoline.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment purports to raise from three cents to four cents the tax on gasoline used by all consumers other than farmers and fishermen, and further purports to exclude those farmers and fishermen from the application of the tax. It has been ruled time and again that no increase can be considered, either of an existing or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown. Further, it is not shown that the increase of one cent, to
four cents, on other classes of consumers would not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Therefore I must declare the amendment out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I
resent some of the remarks made by the Minister of Finance, although perhaps they were not intended as I took them-

In view of what the minister had to say, Mr. Chairman, I am not really surprised that you should rule this amendment out of order without calling upon me to make any remarks. In connection, however, with the amendment moved by an hon. member belonging to another party, the question was asked repeatedly whether anyone else wished to speak to the point of order. My amendment is treated very cavalierly indeed; no one is given a chance to speak to the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The
point of order was raised from the Chair. When the other amendment was before the committee the point of order was raised by the Minister of Finance, and all 'hon. members had an opportunity to speak to it. When the Chair takes it upon itself to decide -that a resolution is out of order, there is no debate; it is a ruling from the Chair.

I have a great deal of sympathy for the minister in the gigantic problem with which he is faced in connection with the budget. I come from a province which in the last war had the greatest per capita enlistment in Canada; I think the figure was 10-8 per cent, and I am sure that if the figures could be obtained by provinces to-day, Manitoba would head the list once more. It has been pointed out repeatedly in this house that a great disparity exists at present between industry and organized labour on the one hand and agriculture on the other. Much as I sympathize with the minister, I submit that there should be some equality of sacrifice at this time. There are no people in Canada more patriotic than those in Manitoba, not only in the matter of enlistments but in the matter of contributing financial assistance to the greatest extent humanly possible. There is, however, certainly nothing like equality of sacrifice at the present time, and hon. gentlemen sitting on the front benches opposite are, to a large extent, responsible for that situation. Even now, as was pointed out last night by many private members, many transportation companies throughout this country use diesel engines entirely. I am told on reliable authority that some gasoline companies in this part of the dominion transport their products in
Special War Revenue Act

vehicles propelled by diesel motors and using crude oil as fuel. These companies, therefore, will not be called upon to pay any tax under this measure. That is most unfair. I understand that fuel for diesel engines is taxed in Ontario. I do not see why these companies should be exempted from this tax, and therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vietoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield):
That resolution No. 6 of the Special War Revenue Act be amended by adding thereto the following words:
Provided, however, that a rebate of the full amount of the tax paid by any farmer or fisherman shall be made upon satisfactory proof that the gasoline upon which the tax was paid was utilized by such farmer or fisherman exclusively for power purposes upon his farm or in his fishing boat; that the difference of revenue be made up by a tax on diesel or fuel oil used for transportation purposes, of three cents per gallon.

It seems to me that this
amendment would involve the question of administration to an even greater degree. Diesel oil is largely used by the fishermen of Nova Scotia and by the merchant marine; and when you interfere with the merchant marine you place it at a disadvantage because it has to meet the competition of the rest of the world. Vessels will not bunker in a country where diesel oil is more expensive than it is in a neighbouring country. For that reason I was very glad that the minister excluded diesel oil from payment of this tax. The deep-sea fishermen of Nova Scotia, especially in the riding which I represent, use boats powered with diesel engines. They work on a cooperative basis; the amount received by the men is determined by the size of the catch and the cost of operating the boat. Therefore I hope the minister will not alter his position in this connection.
We must realize that all exemptions bring about greater administrative costs and reduce the amount of money available for the public service. The amount of money we require is definitely known. These exemptions will not lower the amount required from the people of Canada. With lower overhead costs, however, the people will pay less. When we adjourned last night we were talking about exemptions to the provinces. For the last decade, provinces have been approaching the federal government with the complaint that under our economy they were not obtaining enough money to run their own affairs. There was considerable virtue in their claim, too, up to the time this war broke out. Now, however, the situation is completely changed. The federal government needs money now as it has never needed it before. On the other hand the provinces are reporting surpluses. On account of war-time activities

they have fewer obligations and demands on their treasury, and they have growing revenues, as a result of those war-time activities for which they are not at all responsible.
It occurs to me that we should give some thought to control of the price of gasoline in Canada. It may be that the price of gasoline is too high, and that there is monopoly control. I have some knowledge of gasoline transactions, and it is my belief that that commodity is closely controlled, so far as the eastern coast of Canada is concerned. While there is some indication of importations by certain companies, most of it is sold to them by the one big refining company. We refine crude oil in Nova Scotia, but for years we have been paying more for gasoline in Nova Scotia than is paid in many other parts of Canada. In these days of trial when we must do extreme things to keep the economy of our country on a level basis, it seems to me that we might give consideration to fixing the price of gasoline to be used by our people.
Our western friends seem to be solicitous about the fishermen. They were not so solicitous the other day when they wanted a fifty-cent processing tax on wheat, which would have raised by $1.25 a bag the price of flour used by every fisherman in Canada.
Nonsense.

But they come to us now
and say, "Oh, we put the fishermen in the same category as the farmers of western Canada."
I do think we should not exempt the provincial governments. I believe the federal authority should, especially at this time, reach conclusions on national grounds. This parliament represents every citizen and every province. While the claims of provincial governments are important, they are not the first consideration, nor should they be unduly influential outside their own sphere of government.
If there is going to be any exemption at all, then I do think the farmers and fishermen deserve it, ahead1 of the provincial governments. The minister has shown that this is a national matter, and a critical moment. He has pointed out that, due to conditions, people must make sacrifices and be prepared to pay. Therefore I believe that if there are to be no exemptions at all, it will be better and cost everybody less.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to advise the committee of my ruling in respect of the new amendment. The same ruling applies. In the first place the amendment proposes to impose a new tax of three cents a gallon on diesel or fuel oil used for transportation

purposes. According to May, page 511, this is an increase in an existing tax, or a new or temporary tax for the service of the year.
