speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe that is a proper deduction. There might be amendments which could disturb the resolution before the committee. The Chairman rules only when occasion arises. I do not believe it would be in order to say that nothing would shake the structure of the resolution.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish for one moment to reflect upon the dignity of the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know.

I realize, as the Chairman has stated, that it might be possible to find an amendment which, if it did not shake the provision, would at least disturb it.
I find myself, however, to some extent in agreement with the contention of the Minister of Finance. I believe on second thought-yes, on first thought-that every hon. member realizes the gravity of the situation. That is uppermost in our minds. The challenge with regard to taxation and in connection with war expenditures is to get on with the job, and to meet the whole war situation. No doubt with that in mind the minister has made all possible tests and has studied carefully ways and means by which he might raise this huge budget.
I believe the seriousness of the situation is much more important than some of the representations might indicate. In all fairness I must say I believe the hon. member for Rosthern has advanced splendid reasons why some further consideration might be given by the government. I do not think we are particularly concerned how heated the hon. member might have been, or in what eloquent terms he might have spoken. In my opinion, however, our whole war effort is in some degree affected by the type of taxation we impose. It has been said that equality of sacrifice means equal taxation right along the line, and no exemptions. That sounds very 14873-192
well. But as the hon. member for Rosthern has said-and I believe you will agree, Mr. Chairman-the tax which the farmer pays on gasoline used for power on the farm is about the only tax, in a long list, which cannot be passed on to somebody else. That point must be clear to all.
For instance, the man who drives a motor truck will no doubt feel this imposition very heavily. But if you hire that motor truck to carry the products of your farm or your factory, you will pay the driver an extra amount, and he will see that you do so. You, in turn, will consider the charge quite proper. Then, to some extent the man who drives his automobile from his suburban home to the factory is being cared for. Recent arrangements have been made for a cost-of-living bonus for labouring men. In many places, labour is receiving better wages, and better hourly rates of pay. Other charges against their earnings would soon be brought to the attention of employers by the well-organized unions. Employers, in turn, usually yield, rather than see any more hardship suffered by labour. I am quite in accord with the principle of giving labour a square deal in that regard.
The great mass of taxation raised by this three-cent imposition will be collected from the drivers of motor cars, from those who are driving for pleasure and from tourist traffic. It is true that this three-cent tax will be in some degree an imposition upon any hon. member who takes his family out for a drive, but he can afford to pay it. A man who is driving thirty or forty thousand miles a year can better afford to pay this tax than the man who uses his car to meet the bare necessities of his farm and often runs it only two or three thousand miles a year. I think the gasoline tax is a fair tax if it is not raised to an exorbitant figure. In many of the provinces the tax is quite high, but I still think it is a reasonable and fair tax. Many hon. members use their automobiles a great deal, especially in election years, and if we drive 25,000 or 30,000 miles a year, there is no better way in which we can pay our share of the cost of the roads.
I have no criticism to make of the government for imposing this tax at a time when they are in need of revenue. This tax works out to about fifteen per cent of the cost of the gasoline. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has stated that he uses horses on his farm and implies that horses are cheaper. As one who considers the production of horses a profitable proposition and realizing that this statement might help the horse-breeding indus-

Special War Revenue Act

try, I am glad to see someone advocating the use of horses. However, even though I am a horse man I still use a tractor, as do most modern farmers, in order not to impose too much work upon my horses. I think a tractor can be used economically on a reasonably sized farm.
This tax of approximately fifteen per cent upon a major item of the production cost of the farmer affects not only the individual farmer, it affects the cost of production of many primary products. I am not speaking particularly for those farmers who have sold their horses and have bought gasoline tractors and who may not be in a position this year to utilize horsepower; I am speaking with reference to the gravity of the whole situation. Our farmers are faced with greatly increased rates for labour. Help is difficult to get, and many farmers are letting their horses go and buying tractors because one man on a tractor can do as much work as three men with horses. The maintenance of production is, to my mind, relevant in assisting in connection with the gravity of the whole situation, and this should be considered on that basis if on no other. Not that the farmer has not been receiving enough for what he has been producing, but in order to maintain efficiency of production I suggest that the minister might give serious consideration to this matter. He might let this resolution stand and study some of the proposals that have been embodied in the amendments which have been ruled out of order this afternoon.
In many districts we find the farmers are discouraged, and the Minister of Finance knows this. I am concerned about that; we all are, but I am more concerned with its effect upon the bigger picture, in other words, the gravity of the larger situation. As I have mentioned before in this house, I have picked up some of these slips on the train which tell us not to consume any more butter than we can help. We have a price control board, and we seem to be bending every effort to see that the farmer does not get too much for his bacon or too much for his butter. We are trying to keep prices down in the belief that it offsets a tendency toward inflation. The farmer is the only one who cannot pass these things on to the consumer. He must produce at less than cost, and his labour problem to-day is greater than it has been at any time in the last quarter of a century.
I ask the Minister of Finance to consider this issue, not on its possible reference to class legislation, not on its possible advantages to certain individuals throughout the country, but more especially on its possible effect, in the
^Mr. Rowe.]
long-range point of view, upon our whole war economy. Boats filled with foodstuffs are being sent to the bottom; we have more men in the army and fewer men for production. The day is rapidly approaching when, even though some people may love the horse-drawn system, we shall be forced to put every modern convenience into effect in order to maintain our standard of production and the efficiency in that regard which is necessary for an all-out war effo.rt. What happened in the last great war? It was not long after the war started that prices started sky-rocketing because there was a shortage. It may not be entirely relevant to the issue, but I say that it would be better if hogs were selling at $12 a hundredweight, if butter were five cents a pound higher, if cheese were four or five cents a pound higher, in order to encourage a steady production, than to wait until a shortage occurs and prices skyrocket.
I trust I shall not be misunderstood, but I wish to speak of this matter in the light of the larger picture. To my mind, that is the one fundamental issue before us. We must win this war. We must do this job. We must maintain supplies for our troops overseas. We must be ready to meet the hungry families of Europe immediately after the war. We must be ready to meet the losses that have taken place and will take place on the high seas. I think anyone who has had any experience in agriculture will agree with me when I say that if an attempt is made to encourage our people to go back to the use of horse-drawn implements when there are only about half as many men available, production will be affected materially.
A tax of three cents a gallon is not a great deal to me. I shall have to pay more on what I use in my automobile than for what I use in my tractor, so I shall not suffer particularly. I think I should pay a substantial tax toward our war effort when I use the roads much more than another farmer. Another man may have a tractor which is not yet paid for but which he was forced to buy in order to farm two or three hundred acres because his boy has gone overseas and he cannot hire a man anywhere. To my mind, this is a factor which enters into the picture.
I am speaking on the gravity of the larger picture. I ask the minister to reconsider this tax, not because some of his supporters have risen to oppose this quite heatedly, not because it would please certain farmers in my riding, but because of its effect upon the broader picture. It is highly essential that we go full-steam ahead with our war effort. At a time when labour is hard to get, a reasonable use of mechanical devices such as these new

modem tractors is necessary. The farmer is not making any profit to-day, and I ask the minister to assist him in his war effort by not imposing this fifteen per cent tax upon this most important item of production. In many districts where hydro-power is not available, the farmer must use gasoline for grinding grain, and so forth. I ask the minister to reconsider this tax on the basis of the efficiency of the larger effort.

I had intended to reserve my views on this matter until the bill was brought down when we shall again have an opportunity of discussing this gasoline tax in detail. I wish, however, to declare myself as being in favour of exempting both the farmer and the fisherman. I suggest to the minister that he should consider all the views that have been placed before him and see if it is not possible to make these exemptions.
Having declared my view in that way, I wish to express myself with reference to the practice that has been adopted this afternoon by at least three hon. gentlemen-and I understand there is a fourth on the doorstep-of moving, at this stage of the resolution, amendments which hon. gentlemen know are out of order.
The Chairman said they might be in order.
Which hon. gentlemen, I repeat-my hon. friend is not one of them- know are out of order when they move them.
I resent that statement, Mr. Chairman. I moved an amendment, and I took it from your ruling on a previous amendment that I was in order. I ask the hon. member to withdraw his insinuation.

order, bring it in and make a fiery speech about it. We have, however, wasted a great deal of time this afternoon because certain hon. gentlemen cannot resist the desire to make heroes of themselves by so doing.
I protest, Mr. Chairman, and rise to a point of order. I asked that the hon. member for Parry Sound withdraw the statement which he has just made including motives concerning myself.
He did withdraw it.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member went on to impute motives about making a fiery speech for the benefit of the electors of our constituencies. I was speaking purely from a national point of view on behalf of the agriculturists of the whole country.

speechtext: If no other hon. member desires to speak to the point of order, I am afraid that the last remark of the hon. member stating that hon. members in moving their amendments were prompted by the desire to become heroes in their own ridings is out of order, and I would ask him to withdraw it.

Then let me withdraw that statement, in accordance with the ruling of the Chair. Let me put it in this way. From now on, should we not attempt, with serious war measures of this kind, either to take some care to observe the rules of the house or to amend those rules if, in the view of the majority of the house, amendments of that kind ought to be permitted? I have the greatest sympathy with every hon. member who has spoken in favour of these exemptions to-day. I am for them myself. After all, however, there is the procedure which we can take some greater pains to give heed to, and express our views without acting in an unfair manner or in a manner which is prejudicial to other hon. members who have just as strong views as those expressed by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken before them.

I have an amendment, Mr. Chairman, but I am not going to move it because it may be ruled out of order. My amendment was to exempt soldiers engaged on military duties from the operation of resolution 6. I think that should be done, especially when we know that military camps are scattered all over Canada in out-of-the-way places and getting to them involves considerable travel. I hope that when the bill is brought in, the Minister of Finance will give consideration to exempting from this tax members of his majesty's forces, who, after all, receive only $1.30 a day.
I have a short question to ask of the minister. Will he consider having an inquiry before the banking and commerce committee into the high cost of gasoline in Canada? We had such an inquiry a few years ago. I should like these two points to be considered by the minister before the debate concludes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's first suggestion would not be workable. I do not wish to be raising administrative difficulties all the time, but to do absolute justice, to return taxes to everyone who cannot afford to pay them, would not be administrable. We could not do it at all. You might as well say that the sugar tax should be refunded to people below a certain income. That would probably be fair because it is a consumption tax which bears on people of lower incomes, but we would not be doing the right thing to undertake a system of refunds as impracticable as that. I still repeat that hon. gentlemen must bear in mind the importance of maintaining governmental services in such a condition that the public will have respect for them and have respect for the law. That is a fundamental consideration, and hon. gentlemen must not get away from that.
As to my hon. friend's other suggestion that the matter of gasoline prices be referred to the banking and commerce committee, I shall give it consideration. That is the most I can say. But I do not think it would be practicable to do it this session.

I have
not taken any part in the discussion this afternoon. The minister must be aware from the course of the discussion that there is a substantial opinion in this committee against his proposal, in its entirety, to tax gasoline. I am anxious that these budget resolutions should be put through in order that the bills may be introduced and we may be able to study at first hand their contents. All I am going to ask the minister is this. If he cannot yield at the moment to the arguments which have been made in favour of exemptions or rebates 
from the gasoline tax-perhaps I had better call them proposals because there have been so many of them-and I do not see how he could at the moment yield because in a degree and in principle they would upset his budgetaiy proposals, will he undertake to say to the committee that, in view of the widespread requests and arguments in support of those requests which have been made here yesterday and today to eliminate the gasoline tax on farmers and fishermen, he will review the whole position with his colleagues and announce his decision when he introduces the bill? I do not think I should go any further than that.
I am in this position. I think I can weigh evidence, and judge and see both sides of a question. I know we do not do that in political matters; but I am trying not to treat this matter in a political way or from a partisan standpoint. There are, however, certain arguments in favour of the tax as it is. The minister has stated fairly the reasons which actuated the administration in coming to the conclusion which it did. They have had an effect upon my judgment and my mind, and I am wondering whether they are not the major considerations; as yet I have not arrived at a final conclusion in my own mind in that regard. But the minister, in common with myself, must be aware that there is in this chamber a very large body of opinion which, could it be given effect to in a legal way under the rules of this house, and without the intervention of the whips, would put this proposal as it stands in grave danger of defeat. I may be wrong in my view on that, but I believe that if the whips were taken off, the proposal would be defeated. Although I had not intended to do so, I therefore request, as respectfully as I know how, that the minister and the government review this proposal and let the resolution stand, because of the considerations which have been stated here, and of which he is as fully aware as I am.

I have not spoken on this matter, and I take this opportunity to express my views about it. I find that this is one of the most sensible taxes which has been proposed, and I am sure that if the leader of the opposition had been minister of finance this is the first tax which he would have imposed upon the Canadian taxpayer. It is a tax which is paid according to the consumption of gas. The man who uses ten gallons of gas pays his three cents ten times; if he uses a hundred gallons, he pays it a hundred

times. It is unseen, and it is collected at the source. Therefore, in the first place, it will require no special staff for collection.
I regret, of course, that some farmers, and especially some fishermen, will have to pay the tax. But we cannot forget that the western farmers are supposed to receive $30,000,000.
Thirty-five million.

Yes; I thank my hon. friend for correcting me. This means that they will also make a contribution. Their role must be not only to receive money; they must pay some. In the east the farmers have nothing; they do not get anything, although they need it. In the west they receive subsidies of every kind, and now, not satisfied with that, they will not pay taxation. I find this hard to understand, sir; not because I am not in sympathy with the farmers, and not because I have not a soft spot in my heart for the leader of the opposition. It is not these considerations which influence me; I speak now in support of a fair distribution of taxation. I was opposed to a certain tax proposal which was put before us yesterday, but I am in favour of the one now under consideration- which shows that one can have his own views on different matters.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe) this afternoon made one of the best speeches of his career. But all these speeches, except perhaps that of the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker), who spoke on behalf of the farmers, and certainly that of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), on behalf of the fishermen, were inspired by fear. All the hon. members who have spoken against this tax are afraid to explain it to their own constituents.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Just a minute-when I am through. That is the answer the hon. gentleman gave me when I asked him a question in the middle of his speech. They are afraid to speak to their own constituents and tell them it is their duty to contribute in this way to the war effort.
What will they contribute with?

I am sure the leader of the opposition is afraid to meet the good farmers of York-Sunbury and tell them it is their duty to pay this tax. I am convinced that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe is afraid to meet
his own constituents, the good farmers of western Ontario, and tell them that now is the time for them to make this contribution.
I will run against the hon. member in his own riding.

If my hon. friend comes to speak in my riding he will be welcome, but nobody will listen to him.
Now, sir, the situation is that all this is playing politics. The leader of the opposition is playing politics; so is the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe, a past leader of the conservative party of Ontario. I would not accuse the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), but I might venture to include a number of hon. members, with the exception naturally of my good friend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) whom I do not put in the same class. Let them be courageous and tell their constituents that this does not affect at all the autonomy of their provinces. Let them also approve the minister's proposal. This is a good tax; it is so good that I am sure it does not come from the intelligentsia which surrounds the Minister of Finance. It is good, logical taxation; I approve of it, and I am sure that in their hearts most of the hon. members who have spoken against it cannot say it is bad.

I have listened to the speeches made this afternoon in connection with this gasoline tax, and I must admit that I was not fully convinced of its unfairness until I heard the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Pouliot).
I heartily endorse the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition that the Minister of Finance should reconsider this item. The class of producers upon which this tax would fall are at this time the low bracket producers. I am not unmindful in the least of the seriousness of the problem with which the Minister of Finance is confronted, or of the crisis which faces the dominion and the empire at the present time. As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe) has said, we have a job of work to do, and we must do it. That is paramount to every other consideration. But I do submit, and here I concur in what the leader of the opposition has said, that the Minister of Finance should reconsider this item in its aspect of placing a tax upon gasoline used by the basic producers. As has been said repeatedly, the farmers are not only in the low bracket but they are in the lowest bracket of the producers of wealth in Canada.
They are also filling a present need, and, as has been said this afternoon, they will fill a much more imperative and important need in the weeks and months to come. But these
Special War Revenue Act

farmers are discouraged. I have a seven-page letter from one farmer, and I may say in reply to the hon. gentleman who preceded me, that my remarks are not prompted by fear, nor are my sentiments expressed except on the basis of a realistic knowledge of the condition of the farmers.
The farming communities of Canada are the only communities which, during the last ten years, have adhered to the sound milch-cow economy of the country. In peace time or in war time, it is not a part of the policies of a Liberal government to place taxation on the shoulders of the basic producers. I sympathize with the minister in the problems with which he is confronted, but I am not convinced of the impossibility of his raising revenue without taxing the basic producer. If he wishes to raise revenue on gasoline, let him stand on No. 2 highway any day. The other day I counted within five minutes $35,000 worth of pleasure cars passing a given point. Let him increase the tax on people who waste gas and oil, coming from nowhere and going nowhere, consuming the wealth of the country. But let him not place this burden on the farmer.
Someone says that the farmer does not burn much gas. Well, I do not like to interject a personal reference, and I do so only to illustrate the point I am making. On my own farm we bum from forty to fifty gallons a day to produce a crop of questionable market possibilities. I therefore plead with the minister, and I do so not by means of moving a resolution. That is not the proper way; you cannot get anywhere by bringing in resolutions. I appeal to the minister and his advisers in the civil service to reconsider the imposition of this tax on gasoline used by basic producers, whether they be farmers or fishermen.
Let me go a step further. The Minister of Finance knows quite well, and so does the Minister of Labour, that labour is gradually coming into its own in Canada, particularly labour engaged in war industries, labour with mechanical qualifications. Such labour is in great demand, and as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has said, whether wages are affected by war savings certificates or national defence tax, labour expects an increase in wages to take care of the difference. But these men are coming off the farms of Canada; they are coming off the farms of Ontario. The result is that the farmer cannot procure labour at a price which he can pay out of his product. Drive along the highways of this province, as I did the night before last, and you will see on farm after farm the farmer in a tractor equipped with headlights to enable him to carry on his soil preparation at night-one man working fifteen to sixteen hours a day.

And at the end of every ten hours these tractors have consumed in gasoline tax the equivalent of one dozen eggs collected by his wife that day.
Let us be realistic and consider the farmer's condition from the national standpoint. Money can be raised in other ways. The minister's advisers will tell him a hundred different ways of raising this money without increasing the burden on the low bracket producer. If ever there was a time when the farmer needed every encouragement and cooperation and guidance he can get to help him out of a dilemma and enable him to carry on patriotically, that time is now when we are all making a war effort. A duty rests on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance therefore to reconsider the tax. Let him say to the farmers, "We will help you at least to the extent of eliminating the tax on the low bracket basic producers."
